Here I analyze the effect of the linearly increasing injection rate
on the migration of the stress front. Previously, we used a crossover function
to analyze the early- and late time behavior in the constant injection rate case.
There is a parameter $\delta$ that measures the 'slowness' of the transiotion regime.
The obtained $\delta=0.01$ from the fit to our numerical results was inconsistent
with the field data. To resolve this inconsistency, I do a similar analysis
for fluid injection with linearly increasing rate. The injection condition can be
written as
$$q(t) = m_{q} t$$
where $m_{q}$ is the slope of the linearly increasing injection rate. This loading condition
is also more consistent with the field.

## My half-space code agrees with 3DEC

As I did previously, I use my numerical half-space code to do the simulations.
To be sure that my code works correctly I compare with 3DEC results for stress 
front migration. @fig-comparison-halfspace-3dec shows an agreement between results 
obtained from my code and 3DEC. 


## Dimensional self-similarity analysis produces a super-linear late-time scaling exponent for distance ($\alpha=1.2$)

The similarity variables chanve with the injection condtion, we cannot use the
previously derived variables. Given the nonlinear diffusion equation 
$$
	\frac{k_{n}}{12 \mu} \frac{ \partial }{ \partial x } \left(w^{3} \frac{ \partial w }{ \partial x }  \right)  = \frac{ \partial w }{ \partial t } ,
$$ {#eq-diffusion}
and the linearly increasing injection rate

$$
	- \frac{k_{n}}{12 \mu} w^{3} \frac{ \partial w }{ \partial x }  = m_q t,
$$ {#eq-inj-cond}

the dimensionless similarity variables for the soft asymptotic regime are 

$$
    \theta(\zeta) = \frac{w(x,t) - w_{i}}{\left( m_{q}^{2} t^{3} / a \right) ^{1/5}}, \quad \zeta = \frac{x}{\left( a m_{q}^{3} t^{7} \right) ^{1/5}}
$$ {#eq-similarity}

with

$$
    a = \frac{k_{n}}{12 \mu}.
$$

Compared to the constant rate injection, the only things that changed in the
similarity variables is that $q_{0}$ is replaced by $m_{q}$, and the exponents
of times are increased by $3/5$ and $2/5$ for distance and aperture,
respectively. Thus, the similarity variables show the following scaling in time
of distance $x(t) \sim t^{7/5}$ and of aperture $w(t) \sim t^{3/5}$. 

The soft asymptotic limit is reached at large times when $t \gg t_{c}$ with
$t_{c}$ being the characteristic time. At smaller times $t \leq t_{c}$, the
similarity behavior is governed by linear diffusion where distance aperture
scale proportionally to $t^{1/2}$.

### Derived similarity variables superpose the late-time aperture profiles obtained from a numerical solution

Since I derived the dimensionless variables by hand it would be cautios
to cross-check them with the numerical results of aperture profiles.

```{python}

run = io.read_halfspace(paths.results_dir("halfspace", "linear") / "m_q-1e-08.hdf5")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-similarity
#| fig-cap: Aperture profiles throughout the simulation (a) in dimensional form (b) nondimensionalized with similarity variables for soft asymptotic regime. The dimensionless profiles collapse at late times.

fig = plt.figure(
    figsize=(6.4, 4.8 / 2.5), dpi=95, layout="constrained", clear=True, num=1
)
axes = fig.subplots(1, 2)

sm = plotting.plot_nondimensionalization(
    axes[0], axes[1], run, physics.nondimensionalize_soft, bc="ramp_rate", step=5
)

axes[1].set_xlim(0, 3)
axes[0].annotate("(a)", (-0.15, 1.1), xycoords="axes fraction")
axes[1].annotate("(b)", (-0.15, 1.1), xycoords="axes fraction")

fig.colorbar(sm, ax=axes, label="$t$, [s]", pad=0.02, aspect=10)

fig.canvas.draw_idle()
plt.pause(0.01)
```

@fig-similarity shows both dimensional and dimensionless aperture profiles. As expected, at large times when the aperture gradient is significant the dimensionless aperture profiles superpose better than at smaller times.

### Deriving dimensionless front distance

Using @eq-diffusion and @eq-inj-cond, we can derive the following dimensionless parameters
$$
    w \to \frac{w}{w_{i}}; \quad x \to \frac{x}{x_{c}},\ x_{c} = \left( \frac{a^{2} w_{i}^{7}}{m_{q}} \right)^{1/3}; \quad t \to \frac{t}{t_{c}},\ t_{c} = \frac{x_{c}^{2}}{a w_{i}^{3}} 
$$
where $x_{c}$ and $t_{c}$ are characteristic distance and time, respectively. These characteristic scales can be used to study the evolution of the dimensionless front position across multiple simulations.

## Fitting the crossover function to the numerical data results in $\delta=0.3$, producing "faster" transition than constant injection rate condition

Given that the early-time power-law exponent that describes the migration of
the stress front is 0.5 and the late-time exponent is 1.2 (@eq-similarity),
the crossover function that combines both power-laws separated by $t_{c}$ is
$$
	x_{f}(t) = \frac{A_{\mathrm{early}}t^{0.5}}{1 + (t/t_{c})^{\delta}} + \frac{A_{\mathrm{late}}t^{1.2}}{1 + (t_{c}/t)^{\delta}}.
$$

```{python}

result_dir = paths.results_dir("halfspace", "linear")
mq_values = np.geomspace(1e-14, 1e-8, 7)

runs = [io.read_halfspace(result_dir / f"m_q-{m_q:.0e}.hdf5") for m_q in mq_values]

# Early-time runs need truncated slices (front detection breaks down late);
# later runs are well-behaved over their full range.
CUSTOM_SLICE_FRACTIONS = {0: 5, 1: 2, 2: 2}  # run_index -> keep first 1/N of points


def slice_for_run(i: int, n_points: int) -> slice:
    if i in CUSTOM_SLICE_FRACTIONS:
        return slice(None, n_points // CUSTOM_SLICE_FRACTIONS[i])
    return slice(None, None)


results = [
    analysis.analyze_front(run, stress_front=True, slc=slice_for_run(i, len(run.t)))
    for i, run in enumerate(runs)
]
bc = "ramp_rate"


t_min = runs[0].t[0]
t_max = runs[-1].t[-1]
t_range = np.geomspace(
    t_min / physics.characteristic_time(runs[0].params, bc=bc),
    t_max / physics.characteristic_time(runs[-1].params, bc=bc),
    200,
)

delta = 0.3
front_crossover = math_utils.crossover(
    x=t_range, a=1.9, alpha=0.5, b=1.8, beta=1.2, x0=1, delta=delta
)
```

I did several numerical simulations (using half-space code) with the slope of the
injection rate condition $m_{q}$ varying in the range
$\mathrm{10^{-14}\,m^2/s^2} \leq m_{q} \leq \mathrm{10^{-8}\,m^2/s^2}$. The fit
of the crossover function to the numerical data gives $\delta=0.3$ (see 
below @fig-front). The two asyptotic power-laws are clearly separated by the dimensionless characteristic time $t_{c} = 1$.

Previously with a constant injection rate condition, I obtained
$\delta=0.01$ and the asymptotic scaling exponents were 0.5 and 0.8. The
results here show that the transition between asymptotic regimes is faster in
the linearly increasing injection rate condition.


```{python}
#| label: fig-front
#| fig-cap: Migration of the dimensionless front across simulations with injection rate ramp $m_q$ varying from $\mathrm{10^{-14}\,m^2/s^2}$ to $\mathrm{10^{-8}\,m^2/s^2}$.

fig = plt.figure(
    figsize=(6.4 / 1.3, 4.8 / 1.3), dpi=100, layout="constrained", clear=True, num=1
)
ax = fig.subplots()
for run, result in zip(runs[::1], results[::1]):
    label = rf"$m_q={plotting.sci_latex(run.params.m_q)}\,\mathrm{{m^2 / s^2}},\ \alpha = {result.alpha_emp:.2f}$"

    ax.scatter(
        result.t / physics.characteristic_time(run.params, bc=bc),
        result.y / physics.characteristic_distance(run.params, bc=bc),
        s=5,
        label=label,
    )
ax.plot(
    t_range,
    front_crossover,
    "k--",
    lw=2,
    label=rf"Crossover function, $\delta={delta}$",
)
ax.set(
    xlabel=r"$t / t_c$",
    ylabel=r"$x_f / x_c$",
    title="Stress front evolution",
    xscale="log",
    yscale="log",
)
ax.legend(fontsize="small", frameon=False)
fig.canvas.draw_idle()
plt.pause(0.01)
```

## Fitting to the field data

```{python}

SECONDS_PER_DAY = 86_400


def _to_days(t_sec):
    return t_sec / SECONDS_PER_DAY


crossover_model = analysis.CrossoverModel(alpha_early=0.5, alpha_late=1.2, delta=0.3)
t_s, d_s = io.load("soultz")
soultz = analysis.fit_field_crossover(
    t_s,
    d_s,
    title="Soultz 1993",
    percentile=90,
    t_c=4.5 * SECONDS_PER_DAY,
    model=crossover_model,
    eval_based_envelope=True,
)

t_b, d_b = io.load("basel")
basel = analysis.fit_field_crossover(
    t_b,
    d_b,
    title="Basel 2006",
    percentile=75,
    t_c=3 * SECONDS_PER_DAY,
    model=crossover_model,
    eval_based_envelope=True,
)
```

```{python}
def plot_field_case(
    ax: matplotlib.axes.Axes, field_case: analysis.FieldCase, **set_kwargs
):
    ax.scatter(_to_days(field_case.t), field_case.d, color="tab:gray", s=3)
    ax.scatter(
        _to_days(field_case.t_env),
        field_case.d_env,
        color="k",
        label=f"P{field_case.percentile:g} per {field_case.bin_size} events",
        s=25,
    )
    ax.plot(
        _to_days(field_case.t_fit),
        field_case.d_fit,
        color="tab:blue",
        lw=3,
        label=rf"Crossover, $\delta={field_case.model.delta}$",
    )
    ax.axvline(
        _to_days(field_case.t_c),
        color="k",
        ls=":",
        label=rf"$t_c=\mathrm{{{_to_days(field_case.t_c):.2g}\ days}}$",
    )
    ax.set(
        xlabel="Time [day]", ylabel="Distance [m]", title=field_case.title, **set_kwargs
    )

    idx_tc =  np.searchsorted(field_case.t_fit, field_case.t_c)
    exponent, log_prefactor = np.polyfit(
        np.log(
            _to_days(
                field_case.t_fit[: idx_tc]
            )
        ),
        np.log(field_case.d_fit[: idx_tc]),
        deg=1,
    )
    plotting.slope_triangle(
        ax=ax,
        x0=_to_days(field_case.t_fit[10]),
        slope=round(exponent, 2),
        prefactor=np.exp(log_prefactor + 1),
    )

    ax.spines[["right", "top"]].set_visible(False)
    ax.legend(loc="lower right", framealpha=1, fontsize="small")
    return ax
```
